titre: Thirty Years of Silence Before the Nobel Prize
accroche: In 1951, McClintock demonstrates that genes move around in the genome. Her presentation is met without a single question
contenu_vulgarise:
The kernels on an ear of corn are not all the same color. Some are uniformly pigmented, others carry speckles, streaks, darker sectors, and the pattern changes from one ear to the next.

This was considered an irregularity of no interest. Barbara McClintock devoted decades to it.

## What the speckles signal

A spot on a kernel is a group of cells producing a pigment while their neighbors do not. Since all descend from a single initial cell, something changed during development.

McClintock links these patterns to what she observes under the microscope on corn chromosomes, of which she is one of the best specialists.

Her conclusion, in the 1940s and 1950s, contradicts what genetics takes for granted. Certain elements of the genome do not stay in place: they cut themselves out and reinsert elsewhere. By settling in the middle of a pigmentation gene, such an element deactivates it; by leaving again, it reactivates it. The color of the kernel records these movements.

Genes that move, in a genome that had been pictured as a string of fixed beads.

## The reception

She presents these results in 1951 at a symposium at Cold Spring Harbor. The presentation is followed by silence.

The work is not refuted; it is set aside. Several reasons add up. Corn is not the organism on which genetics is making its advances at the time. The reasoning, based on color patterns and cytology, takes effort to read. And the result contradicts a convenient picture.

McClintock stops publishing on the subject for years, while continuing her experiments.

## The turnaround

Recognition does not come from a rereading of her papers. It comes from an independent discovery.

In the late 1960s and in the 1970s, mobile elements are identified in bacteria, then in the fruit fly, with the tools of the emerging field of molecular biology. The phenomenon ceases to be a curiosity of corn and becomes general.

Attention then turns back to her work. She is awarded the Nobel Prize in 1983, more than thirty years after the symposium.

We now know that these mobile elements occupy a considerable fraction of genomes, our own included.

## What the delay teaches

The easy moral would be that a brilliant woman was ignored by a sexist community, and the sexism of the era is real. But the precise mechanism deserves better.

A result is not accepted because it is demonstrated. It is accepted when the community has the means to redo it, and these means, for mobile elements, arrived only twenty years later.

repere.texte: McClintock presents her results on mobile elements at the Cold Spring Harbor symposium in 1951: the presentation is met with silence. The Nobel Prize is awarded to her in 1983.
repere.source: Ravindran, “Barbara McClintock and the discovery of jumping genes,” PNAS, 109, 2012

carte.punch: A result is not accepted because it is demonstrated, but when it can be redone.
carte.idee: McClintock reads in the speckles of corn kernels that certain elements of the genome move. Presented in 1951, the result is set aside for twenty years, until these elements are found in bacteria.

quiz.question: Why did her results remain without effect for twenty years?
choix: Because an error had been found in her microscope observations
Because she had chosen not to publish them during her lifetime
Because the community did not yet have the means to find the phenomenon elsewhere
Because corn does not have the same mechanisms as other organisms
quiz.explication: The work was published and was never refuted: it was set aside. Mobile elements were accepted only once they were found in bacteria and then in the fruit fly, with the tools of molecular biology. They proved, moreover, to be general, and occupy a considerable share of our own genome.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, how does a mobile element deactivate a pigmentation gene, according to McClintock?
choix: By permanently destroying the gene through an irreversible mutation
By settling in the middle of the gene, which becomes active again when the element leaves
By duplicating itself to take the place of two neighboring genes
By blocking the division of the cell carrying the gene
quiz_supplementaire.explication: By settling in the middle of a pigmentation gene, the mobile element deactivates it; when it leaves, the gene becomes active again. The color of the kernel thus records these movements.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does McClintock first present her results on mobile elements?
choix: At the presentation of her Nobel Prize in 1983
In an article published in Nature in 1965
At a symposium at Cold Spring Harbor in 1951
At a conference at Columbia University in 1948
quiz_supplementaire.explication: She presents these results in 1951 at a symposium at Cold Spring Harbor. The presentation is followed by silence, the work being not refuted but set aside.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which organisms are mobile elements rediscovered in the late 1960s and in the 1970s, reviving interest in McClintock's work?
choix: In humans only, thanks to genome sequencing
In other varieties of corn, grown in South America
In bacteria, then in the fruit fly
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the late 1960s and in the 1970s, mobile elements are identified in bacteria, then in the fruit fly, with the tools of the emerging field of molecular biology: the phenomenon ceases to be a curiosity of corn.
